questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: An outlier and a valid extreme
questions.learningObjective: Identify a valid extreme
questions.stem: Among elevations 1900, 2000, 2100, 2050 m in a mountainous region, which is most likely a valid extreme?

options.text: 1900, because it is the lowest.
options.misconception: flags the minimum as an error

options.text: None, because all are too close to be extremes.
options.misconception: denies valid extremes can be close

options.text: 2000, because it is the average.
2100, because it is the highest plausible value.

questions.explanation: 2100 is the highest value and still plausible for a mountainous region, so it is a valid extreme.
questions.hint: Consider plausibility for the region.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why distance-based methods need a common scale
questions.learningObjective: Explain why scaling is needed before kNN
questions.stem: Explain why a cartographer must scale features before running kNN on elevation and aspect.

answer.exemplar: Without scaling, elevation's larger range dominates the distance, so neighbours are chosen mainly by elevation and aspect is ignored.

questions.explanation: Unscaled elevation dominates distance, making aspect irrelevant to neighbour selection.
questions.hint: Larger range means larger distance contribution.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why gradient methods need a common scale
questions.learningObjective: Explain why scaling is needed before gradient descent
questions.stem: Explain why a cartographer must scale features before gradient descent on elevation and aspect.

answer.exemplar: Scaling makes the loss surface more spherical, so a single learning rate descends efficiently in all directions instead of zigzagging.

questions.explanation: Scaling sphericalises the loss surface, improving gradient descent efficiency.
questions.hint: Spherical surfaces converge faster.

questions.stem: Explain why context matters when deciding whether a value is an outlier.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The ordinal imputation trap
questions.learningObjective: Summarise the ordinal imputation trap
questions.stem: The ordinal imputation trap occurs when:

options.text: Zero imputation inflates the variance.
Mode imputation removes the most common category.
Median imputation always returns a float.
Mean imputation creates values outside the allowed ordinal levels.

questions.explanation: Mean imputation on ordinal data can produce values that are not valid levels, creating nonexistent categories.
questions.hint: The mean may not be a valid level.
